summary: Explores issues in registering internationalized domain names. The large set of allowed characters can cause confusion between similar-looking names, so registries need rules that disallow some combinations. The memo suggests mechanisms for defining such rules across many languages, including methods adapted from Chinese, Japanese, and Korean. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Some letters from different alphabets look the same, and a trickster could use them to fake a website name. This memo suggests rules for registries to stop that.

questions: how to prevent domain name spoofing
subtitle: Rules for preventing confusion and fraud in internationalized domain names.

tldr.problem: Internationalized domain names (IDNs) allow any Unicode character in domain names, opening the door to confusion: the Cyrillic letter A looks identical to the Latin letter A, and a trickster can register nearly-identical names to phish users. Registries need rules to block dangerous combinations.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC proposes a framework for defining and implementing registration restrictions. Registries create language tables that specify which characters are allowed and which variants (lookalike characters) are treated as equivalent. A registration algorithm called CreateBundle groups all variant forms together, blocking competing registrations of lookalike names.
tldr.outcome: Registries can protect users by defining rules that reflect each language's legitimate character repertoire, blocking variant and lookalike registrations, and publishing tables so users and tool authors know what is allowed.

facts.label: Table format
facts.value: Unicode codepoints with pipe-separated variant lists

today: RFC 4290 is Informational and provides the foundational framework for IDN registration practices. ICANN maintains the IANA language variant table registry based on these principles, and most registries now implement variant restrictions following these guidelines or adapted variants of them.

sections.title: The Lookalike Problem in IDN Registration
sections.content:
Internationalized domain names (IDNs) allow non-ASCII characters from any language in domain names. This is a powerful feature, but it creates a new security risk: characters that look identical or nearly identical across different alphabets and scripts. For example, the Cyrillic letter 'A' (U+0410) and the Latin letter 'A' (U+0041) look the same in most fonts. A registrant could register 'pаypal.com' (with Cyrillic 'a') to look like 'paypal.com' (with Latin 'a'), phishing users who mistype or misjudge which version they visited.

The original DNS hostname rules (LDH convention: letters, digits, hyphen) avoided this by restricting to ASCII. IDNs cannot use such a global restriction because different languages require different character sets. Instead, registries must define language-specific rules that allow legitimate characters but block lookalike registrations.
sections.eli5: In English domain names, you can only use a-z, 0-9, and hyphens. With international names, you can use any character, but that means bad guys can register names that look like real ones to trick people.

sections.title: Characters, Variants, and Registrations
sections.content:
This RFC defines key concepts for managing lookalike characters. A base character is one that a registry allows in registrations. A variant is a character or string that looks similar or equivalent to a base character. For example, if a registry allows the Latin letter 'a' as a base character, it might define Cyrillic 'a' or Greek 'a' as variants.

When a user requests to register a domain name, the registry checks every character. If all characters are base characters, the registration can proceed. When it does, the registry creates a registration bundle—a group of related domain names. The bundle includes the base registration (what the user requested) plus all names that would result from substituting variant characters. For example, if the user registers 'example.com', the bundle might also include 'exаmple.com' (with Cyrillic 'a'), 'еxample.com', and so on. Only the base registration enters the DNS; the others are reserved, preventing someone else from registering lookalike variants.
sections.eli5: When you register a name, the system finds all similar-looking versions and blocks them so nobody else can register those tricks. This stops the bad guys before they start.

sections.title: Language Tables and the JET Guidelines
sections.content:
The best existing system for handling IDN registration restrictions is the JET Guidelines, developed for Chinese, Japanese, and Korean (CJK) domain names. This RFC extends those principles to other languages. A language table published by a registry lists the allowed characters and their variants. The format is simple: each line names a base character, followed by a pipe and a list of colon-separated variants.

The JET Guidelines distinguish between scripts (collections of characters) and languages (subsets of a script used for a specific language). This RFC applies the same concept: a 'language' is defined by a code and a character list, which a TLD registry or language authority maintains. Different registries can have different tables for the same script, reflecting the different needs of different communities.
sections.eli5: Each registry publishes a list saying 'these letters are OK to use, and these other letters look too similar so they're blocked.' Different countries can have different lists based on what their language needs.

sections.title: The CreateBundle Algorithm
sections.content:
The CreateBundle algorithm is the core registration mechanism. When a registrant requests a domain name, the registry runs this algorithm:

First, the registry splits the requested name into individual characters and checks each one against the language table. If any character is not a base character, registration fails immediately.

Next, the registry runs the IDNA ToASCII operation (converting to punycode format for the DNS). If this step fails, registration fails.

Then, for each character in the name, the registry builds a set containing the character and all its variants. It creates every possible combination by substituting variants, building a temporary bundle of partial label strings.

Finally, for each candidate label in the temporary bundle, the registry runs ToASCII. If it succeeds, the label is added to the final registration bundle. This leaves a bundle of zero or more names: at minimum the base registration, and possibly additional variant names.

The base registration and all variant labels are timestamped and stored. If a later registrant tries to register any name in the bundle, the system rejects it (first-come, first-served).
sections.eli5: The algorithm is simple: take the name the user typed, find all lookalike versions, convert them all to the DNS format, and block all of them. That way nobody else can fake that name later.

sections.title: Attacks and Limitations
sections.content:
Even with registration restrictions, lookalike attacks remain possible. No realistic set of rules can eliminate all confusion: in ASCII alone, the digit '1' and lowercase 'l' can be confused in some fonts. IDN restrictions reduce but do not eliminate risk.

The RFC identifies specific threats: an attacker can register an unrestricted lookalike if no variant rule covers that specific pair of characters, or if a registry simply fails to implement restrictions. Registries that allow unrestricted character registration are most vulnerable.

The restrictions also help with secondary issues beyond presentation: they improve database lookups, reduce whois query confusion, and simplify administration. A registrant who registers a name knows which variant strings are reserved, avoiding disputes later.

The RFC emphasizes that registries must choose their character sets and variant rules wisely, often consulting with language experts and community stakeholders. The rules are not one-size-fits-all; they reflect each language and community's needs.
sections.eli5: Even with rules, some trickery is still possible if someone is clever enough. But good rules stop the obvious fakes and make it much harder for bad guys to succeed.

sections.title: Publishing and Maintaining Variant Tables
sections.content:
IANA maintains a registry of language variant tables, administered by ICANN. A TLD registry can submit a variant table for approval. The table must identify itself with:

The submitting registry name (usually the TLD itself), a language or script designation, a version number, and a date. Character are identified by Unicode code points in U+xxxx format (e.g., U+0041 for Latin A).

For simplicity, a registry can define a table with no variants: just a list of allowed base characters and no variant mappings. This is the 'no-variants' case. The CreateBundle algorithm simplifies to just checking that all characters are valid and that IDNA conversion succeeds.

The RFC notes that many scripts already have variant definitions from Unicode itself (for example, uppercase versus lowercase, or typographic width variants). The Nameprep algorithm used by IDNA maps these automatically during lookup. The RFC recommends that registries restrict registrations to IDNA base characters only, so registrants see exactly what they registered, and lookup variants are handled transparently by Nameprep.
sections.eli5: Registries publish their tables so everyone knows the rules. Simple registries just have a list of allowed letters. Complex ones define lookalike pairs. IANA keeps them all organized.
